HC-MoE v7: The Analysis Restricted to Q75

Higher Criticism over the upper quartile of layers — every result in the series recomputed on that slice
September 15, 2026 · v7 · corrected October 4, 2026 (v7.1)
Abstract. This version redoes the whole analysis with HC computed over the Q75 upper-layer subset rather than the full network, following the suggestion that Q75 is where the signal lives. The recommendation holds, and for a better reason than the one given. At the nominal floor Q75 raises tier-A cells from 5 to 13 and mean |r| from 0.0466 to 0.0735; once the effective sample sizes measured in the 26_09_03 drop are applied, Q75 still leads every other subset with 6 tier-A cells against the full network's 1. The stated rationale — that Q75 boosts positively-correlated cases — is largely right (16 of 19 such cells gain magnitude, mean +0.0453) and is not regression to the mean (corr with the starting value +0.10), but it is asymmetric: negative cells gain almost nothing (+0.0043), so part of what looks like a boost is a global shift toward positive that flips 10 of 36 cells. Qwen becomes unambiguous — all nine benchmarks positive, seven tier A at the nominal floor, top cell Qwen/competition_math at +0.163 (+0.29 sd of Intelligence Gain in the top HC decile) — and ERNIE is transformed, from a mean inside the floor at the full network to +0.061 here. Two costs come with the restriction: the estimator spread widens to 0.0296 against a 0.0193 floor, and ERNIE's gain does not survive partialling on Fisher (-0.0044), so for that family the depth signal is dense rather than sparse.
Correction (v7.1, October 4, 2026). Earlier versions of this report, back to v5, said Gemma was the only family whose small model is dense, and used that to explain Gemma's inverted sign. That was wrong: all four small models are dense (Qwen3-0.6B, ERNIE-4.5-0.3B-Base, Gemma 4 E2B, LFM2-700M). Every family therefore has the same design — HC from the routing of a large MoE model, compared against a dense small baseline — and the dense baseline cannot explain any difference between families. This version corrects the family table, removes that confound from the Gemma findings, and adds an architectural reading of the family differences in section 2. No number in the report changes.

1. Research goals and where the study stands

The two primary questions

  1. Does HC track token difficulty? r(HC, CEbig) and r(HC, CEsmall), answered first.
  2. Does HC track Intelligence Gain? r(HC, IG), IG = CEsmall − CEbig.

Null estimator, HC variant, control and statistic remain secondary axes — checks on those two answers rather than findings of their own. What has changed is that the layer subset is no longer a secondary axis at all: it has been fixed at Q75 and every number in this report is computed on that slice.

The change, and what it rests on

Earlier versions computed HC over the full network and treated Q50–Q95 as an axis to scan. This version fixes the slice at Q75, the upper quartile of layers. The case for it, on the numbers in section 4: at the nominal floor Q75 carries 13 tier-A cells against the full network's 5, and under the measured-ESS correction it carries 6 against 1 — the best of all six subsets on both counts.

Fixing the slice does not make the selection go away, it makes it explicit. Q75 was chosen after seeing all six subsets, so nothing in this report is pre-registered and the nominal p-values do not account for that choice. Section 4 gives the Šidák-adjusted threshold (|z| > 2.32), tests the stated rationale directly, and says what it would take to pre-register Q75 properly. Read this report as a well-motivated re-analysis of one slice, not as confirmation that the slice was right.

Main findings so far

What the project holds after seven reports, not a summary of this one. Each claim carries its evidence tier and the version it was established in, so a claim standing since v3 reads differently from one that appeared this cycle. Tier-C beliefs are not listed here — they are in the open column of section 12. Two qualifications attach to every Intelligence Gain claim below and travel with them: corr(gap, IG) = 0.96, so at summary level the IG signal is very nearly the difficulty gap; and no block-bootstrap null has yet been run on the Q75 slice itself.

New in v7: the family sign split largely disappears on the CE targets at Q75 — Gemma moves from clearly negative on both to near zero, so all four families now agree in direction on difficulty.

Not re-testable at Q75 — neither the pmin control nor InvMinP exists at that slice in this drop, so this belief rests entirely on full-network evidence.

The validation register behind those findings, recorded as each check ran rather than written afterwards. Three of the thirteen core checks come back partial at this slice, and one check outside the core set has never run at all. The block-bootstrap null ran on full-network HC rather than Q75, so the 2.29× deflation used here is transferred rather than measured. Control retention covers Fisher but not | p_min, which does not exist at Q75 in this drop — so the multi-expert claim in the register above rests entirely on full-network evidence. The difficulty-gap confound is measured at summary level only. Separately, and outside the core list, no rank or winsorised check has ever run, so it remains unknown whether these Pearson correlations describe the corpus or a handful of outlier tokens. The first two are the top of section 13.

All four small models are dense. HC is always computed from the large MoE model's routing, and IG always compares that model with a dense baseline from the same family, so the design is uniform. What varies is the large model's routing design and how much compute it has per token relative to its small partner. The last column of the table is that ratio. Specs are from the model cards. Gemma 4 E2B uses per-layer embeddings: 2.3B parameters do the computation and a further 2.8B are embedding tables used as lookups, so its compute is counted at 2.3B.

Why the families differ: an architectural reading

With the dense-baseline explanation gone, two architectural differences remain that could account for why the families behave so differently. Both are hypotheses (tier C) — four families are not enough to separate them — but they make specific, testable predictions.

FamilyActive ratioRouted experts per layerShared pathmean r(HC, IG) at Q75Survives Fisher control?
Qwen5.5×128 (top-8)none+0.1246yes, 60% retained
ERNIE10×64 (top-6)2 shared experts+0.0615no (−0.0044)
Liquid~2×32 (top-4)none; conv blocks−0.0184—
Gemma1.7×128 (top-8)1 shared expert−0.0368partly, 39% retained

1. A large compute gap is needed for a positive association. The two families whose large model applies 5× or more of its small partner's per-token parameters, ERNIE (10×) and Qwen (5.5×), are positive. The two with a gap of about 2×, Liquid (2.0×) and Gemma (1.7×), are near zero or negative, and Gemma, with the smallest gap, is the most negative. Total-parameter ratios give the same split (ERNIE 70×, Qwen 51×, Liquid 11×, Gemma 4.9×). The reading: a token with anomalous routing leans hard on a few specialised experts, and that marks extra gain only when the large model has substantial extra capacity to spend on it. The ordering is not perfect. ERNIE has the larger gap but Qwen the stronger association, so the rank correlation across the four families is 0.8 (p = 0.2): a pattern, not evidence. Point 2 accounts for the top of the order. The gap also does not explain why Gemma goes below zero rather than to zero like Liquid. Two Gemma-specific candidates remain: its always-active shared expert, and E2B's per-layer embeddings, which give the small model 2.8B parameters of token-specific lookup capacity that a compute ratio does not count.

2. Routing design sets whether the signal is sparse. HC is built to detect a few strong departures among many tests. Qwen gives it the most to work with: 128 routed experts and no shared expert, so every feed-forward computation goes through the router, and the signal stays sparse under the Fisher control. ERNIE's two always-active shared experts carry general-purpose computation outside the router, which fits a routing departure that is broad rather than sparse; it vanishes under the Fisher control. Liquid has only 32 experts per layer, a quarter of Qwen's and Gemma's, which costs HC much of its power, and part of its backbone is convolution rather than attention.

What the earlier reports said instead. v5–v7 attributed Gemma's inversion either to a dense small model (wrong: all four are dense) or to its shared expert absorbing baseline predictability. The shared expert remains a candidate, but ERNIE has two shared experts and is positive, so a shared path alone does not produce an inversion. The within-family test in section 13 separates the compute gap from Gemma-specific causes.

Data integrity: 0 missing grid combinations, so no mean below is shifted by a hole. One column, Avg_Inverse_Min_P, overflows at 8.08e298; it is a descriptive column only and no statistic in this report derives from it.

The correlations in this drop come with an iid Monte-Carlo null: |r| > 0.01934 at p < 0.05 and 0.02541 at p < 0.01, from correlating two independent normal sequences of length 10,000. Token streams are not independent, so that floor is permissive.

The deflation measured on the next drop can be bridged onto this one, and it costs a factor of about 2.3

The 26_09_03 permutation drop measured effective sample sizes directly from the within-passage autocorrelation, on the same four families and nine benchmarks. Its median deflation on the IG target is 2.29×. Applying each cell's own measured factor to the nominal 10,000 here gives an equivalent ESS and a widened floor: at the median, |r| > 0.02968 instead of 0.01934, a factor of 1.51.

Under that correction Q75 keeps 27 of 36 cells outside the floor and 6 tier-A cells, down from 13 at the nominal floor. The tier table in section 14 carries both gradings side by side so the cost of the correction is visible per cell rather than only in aggregate.

What the bridge assumes. The deflation was measured on the full-corpus run with HC computed over the whole network, and is applied here to HC computed over Q75 on a 10,000-token subsample. That assumes the autocorrelation of the loss series carries over (reasonable — it is a property of the text, and the losses are the same quantity) and that restricting HC to upper layers does not change the autocorrelation of the HC series much (untested). It is a sensitivity, not a measurement. The honest reading is that the truth lies between the two gradings, closer to the bridged one.

Figure 1 — Null calibration on the Q75 slice (mandatory figure)

Fisher-z across the 432 Q75 IG configurations at nominal n. δ0 = +3.13, σ0 = 10.9 against the theoretical N(0,1). The excess dispersion is lower than the full network's 12.0 but still large, and most of what remains is real between-family heterogeneity — section 5 shows the families differ in sign.

BH-FDR on those z-scores leaves 351 of 432 configurations at q < 0.05. The twelve estimator × variant configurations behind each cell have a participation ratio of 1.17 of 12 (mean pairwise r = 0.92), so the 432 configurations amount to about 42 independent tests. That redundancy is inflated multiplicity for counting purposes and intended robustness for the estimator design; both readings are used below and neither cancels the other.

Q75 is the best subset on both gradings — which is a stronger argument than the one it was chosen for

Running the identical battery on each of the six subsets and grading twice — once at the nominal floor, once with each cell's measured deflation applied — puts Q75 at the top of both columns. At the nominal floor it ties Q85 at 13 tier-A cells; under the bridged ESS it leads outright with 6. The full network, which the series headlined for five versions, comes last on both.

This matters because it is a different argument from the one in the suggestion. “Q75 boosts the positive cases” is a statement about direction; “Q75 survives an honest deflation better than any other subset” is a statement about evidence, and it is the one that justifies fixing the slice.

Figure 2 — Evidence by layer subset, graded two ways

Ordered dimension, so lines. Both tier-A curves peak at Q75–Q85 and the bridged one peaks at Q75 alone. The third line shows that the count of cells clearing the widened floor is nearly flat from Q75 up, so the tier differences come from robustness and sign agreement rather than from bare significance.

The stated rationale is broadly right, but the boost is asymmetric

The suggestion was that Q75 boosts the signal of every case with a positive correlation. Tested directly on the 19 cells that are positive at the full network: 16 of 19 gain magnitude, by a mean of +0.0453. That part holds, and it is not a statistical artifact of the kind that usually produces such patterns — the correlation between a cell's full-network value and its change is +0.10, so this is not regression to the mean.

The qualification is symmetry. The 17 cells that are negative at the full network gain almost nothing in magnitude (+0.0043, against +0.0453 for the positives). So Q75 does not amplify signal in general; it shifts the whole grid toward positive by a mean of +0.0303, which raises the positives and pulls the negatives toward zero. 10 of 36 cells change sign in the process. Per family the shift is Qwen +0.0708, ERNIE +0.0600, Gemma +0.0132, Liquid -0.0229.

The practical consequence is narrow but worth stating: a cell that is positive at Q75 and was negative at the full network has not been strengthened, it has been moved. Gemma is where this bites — its magnitude actually falls slightly at Q75 (-0.0029) even though its signed mean rises, because its correlations are negative and the shift is eroding them.

Figure 3 — The boost is not symmetric

Mean change in magnitude moving from the full network to Q75, split by the cell's sign at the full network. Positive cells gain +0.0453; negative cells gain +0.0043. If Q75 amplified signal as such, these bars would be similar.

The selection is real and unadjusted. Q75 is the arg-max subset in only 11% of cells — Q50 holds that title in 39% — so Q75 is not where most individual cells peak; it is where the grid is strongest. The six subsets are nested and correlated at a mean pairwise r of 0.80, worth 1.40 independent looks rather than six, and the Šidák-adjusted threshold for picking one of them is |z| > 2.32. What would pre-register it: fix Q75, GMM and the standard variant in advance, then re-run the grid on a disjoint sample of each corpus. That experiment is first in section 13.

Q1 — at Q75, HC tracks difficulty in every family and in the same direction

Mean |r| is 0.0617 against CEbig (25 of 36 cells outside the nominal floor) and 0.0687 against CEsmall (28 of 36). Both are larger than at the full network.

The more interesting change is that the family sign split largely disappears on the CE targets. At the full network Gemma ran negative against both (−0.034 and −0.055); at Q75 it runs +0.0135 against CEbig and -0.0121 against CEsmall, essentially at the floor. Every family is now positive or null on CEbig: Qwen +0.0367 p<0.01, Liquid +0.0740 p<0.0001, ERNIE +0.0142, Gemma +0.0135. Upper-layer routing anomalies mark hard tokens in all four architectures; it is only the difference between the two models that still splits by family.

Qwen keeps the asymmetry that generates its IG result, and at Q75 it is wider: +0.0367 p<0.01 against the large model's own loss but +0.1025 p<0.0001 against the small model's, a gap of +0.0658 against +0.039 at the full network.

Figure 4 — What HC tracks at Q75, by family

Family means over 108 configurations each. Dashed lines are the nominal ±0.0193 floor. Compare with the full network, where Gemma's blue and red bars were both clearly negative: at Q75 only the green IG bar keeps the inversion.

Q2 — IG at Q75, with Qwen unambiguous and ERNIE transformed

Mean |r| against IG is 0.0735, up from 0.0466 at the full network, with 26 of 36 cells showing all twelve configurations agreeing on sign and tiers of 13 A / 12 B / 11 C at the nominal floor (6 A under the bridged ESS).

Qwen. All nine benchmarks positive, seven of them tier A, mean +0.1246 p<0.0001 — more than double its full-network +0.054. The top cell, Qwen/competition_math, reaches r = +0.1628 (95% CI +0.1437 to +0.1818 at nominal n; +0.1294 to +0.1959 at the bridged ESS), which is +0.29 sd of Intelligence Gain in the top HC decile and 2.7% of its variance. This is the clearest result the series has produced.

ERNIE. At the full network ERNIE averaged +0.0014, inside the floor, and had zero tier-A cells; at Q75 it averages +0.0615 p<0.0001 with four. That is the single largest change the restriction produces, and it means the near-zero ERNIE result reported through v5 and v6 was an artifact of where HC was computed. But see the control check below before reading it as a routing finding.

Gemma and Liquid. Gemma stays inverted at -0.0368 p<0.01, slightly weaker than its full-network −0.050. Liquid moves from +0.005 to -0.0184, crossing zero but staying near the floor either way. The grand mean over all four, +0.0327, is still cancellation and still should not be quoted.

The IG correlation is still not separated from the difficulty gap. At Q75, corr(rsmall − rbig, rIG) = 0.962, essentially unchanged from the full network's 0.95. Restricting the layers does not touch this: the defensible phrasing remains “HC predicts where the small model struggles more than the large one”.

Secondary axis: the controls, and what they do to ERNIE

ERNIE's Q75 gain is dense, not sparse — it does not survive partialling on Fisher

Conditioning on the Fisher combination asks whether HC is doing something a dense routing-elevation statistic cannot. At Q75 the four families answer very differently:

Qwen +0.1246 p<0.0001 → +0.0746 p<0.0001, retaining 60% — the signal is genuinely sparse. Gemma -0.0368 p<0.01 → -0.0145, retaining 39%. ERNIE +0.0615 p<0.0001 → -0.0044 — the entire correlation disappears and changes sign.

So the most dramatic beneficiary of the Q75 restriction is also the one whose gain is not a sparse-departure effect. ERNIE's upper-layer routing does predict Intelligence Gain, but through a broad elevation in routing p-values that the Fisher statistic already captures. HC adds nothing there. Qwen's retention of 60% is the only clean sparse result at Q75.

Figure 6 — What survives conditioning, at Q75

Raw against the Fisher-conditioned correlation and against HC recomputed without its strongest expert. Floor at ±0.0193. Qwen keeps most of its signal under both; ERNIE's vanishes under Fisher. The | p_min control is not available at Q75 in this drop.

Retention is only interpretable when the raw correlation is outside the floor. Liquid's raw Q75 mean is -0.0184, inside it, so its nominal retention of 175% is an artifact of a near-zero denominator and is not reported as a finding. The same caution applies to ERNIE's negative retention: what is meaningful there is the absolute value, -0.0044, not the ratio.

Secondary axes: null estimator and HC variant

Material estimator effect: GLM sits +0.0206 from the others and the spread across estimators is 0.0296 in r (permutation p = 0.000) -- at or beyond the 0.0193 noise floor, so a reader could reach a different conclusion depending on the estimator chosen. Show the per-estimator breakdown, say which estimator each headline number came from, and treat the divergence as a result in its own right: it says something about the null-estimation step, not only about the routing signal.

Direction, which the verdict omits: GLM sits -0.0206 below the other five. And the restriction makes this worse, not better — the spread widens from 0.0252 at the full network to 0.0296 at Q75, against an unchanged 0.0193 floor. Per family: Gemma 0.0653, Qwen 0.0543, ERNIE 0.0275, Liquid 0.0339. Fixing the layer slice has not fixed the null-estimation problem, and a reader handed only the GLM fits would still reach different conclusions.

Pooled over four families and nine benchmarks at Q75. The span of 0.0296 from GMM to GLM is half again the 0.0193 floor.

Figure 8 — Estimator effect within each family at Q75

Split by family. Liquid (purple) is flattest, as at the full network; Gemma and Qwen move most.

Broadly consistent across variants: spread 0.0098 in r (largest deviation hat, +0.0049; permutation p = 0.001), still inside the 0.0193 noise floor. Note it; do not requalify the findings. Standard averages +0.0376 p<0.0001 against hat's +0.0279 p<0.01. The spread has grown from 0.0038 at the full network to 0.0098 here — still comfortably inside the floor, but worth watching if the series settles on Q75.

Restricting to Q75 reorders the benchmarks, and lambada is the casualty

At the full network the loudest benchmarks were lambada (0.0669) and competition_math (0.0667) and the quietest was hellaswag. At Q75 the ranking is different: competition_math leads at 0.1115, followed by fineweb-edu (0.0816) and pg19 (0.0808), while lambada falls to last (0.0547) — from loudest to quietest.

That reversal is the sharpest single consequence of the restriction and it is not noise: lambada is the one benchmark whose signal lives at the full network and decays monotonically with depth. Anyone reading the earlier reports, where lambada carried the headline Qwen result, should note that at Q75 Qwen/lambada is still strong (+0.1408 p<0.0001) but no longer exceptional — it is now the fourth of Qwen's nine rather than the first.

The dataset factor remains far beyond the floor (spread 0.0744, permutation p = 0.0010) and 7 of 9 benchmarks are still split — two or more families outside the floor in opposite directions. The one aligned benchmark at Q75 is lambada, where all four families agree in sign; at the full network that distinction belonged to hellaswag. In both cases the aligned benchmark is the quietest one, which is the same pattern noted in v6: where there is little signal, the families stop disagreeing.

What is specific to Qwen

Qwen is the study's clean result and Q75 is where it is cleanest: every benchmark positive, seven tier A at the nominal floor and five surviving the bridged ESS, and a sparse signal that keeps most of its magnitude when the dense component is partialled out. Architecture: Qwen3's MoE has 128 routed experts, top-8, and no shared expert, so every feed-forward computation goes through the router. That gives a sparse routing statistic the most to see and the most p-values per token. Its compute gap over the dense Qwen3-0.6B baseline is substantial (3.3B against 0.6B, 5.5×) but smaller than ERNIE's, so Qwen's lead over ERNIE points to routing design rather than compute. Confounded by: its estimator spread, the second worst at Q75, so the size of the effect still depends on which null fit was used.

What is specific to ERNIE

ERNIE is the family the restriction changes most, and the change does not survive scrutiny. Its mean goes from inside the floor at the full network to clearly positive at Q75, but conditioning on Fisher removes all of it, so what upper-layer HC detects in ERNIE is a broad routing elevation rather than a sparse departure. Architecture: 64 routed text experts, top-6, plus two always-active shared experts, against a dense 0.3B baseline (10× active parameters). The shared experts do general-purpose computation outside the router, which fits a routing signal that is broad rather than sparse: what remains in the router departs from null across many experts at once. Confounded by: the 70× total-parameter gap, which makes IG large on nearly every token so that its magnitudes are not comparable with the other families', and the shared experts, which are not separated from the routed ones in the HC computation.

What is specific to Gemma

Gemma is the family Q75 does not help. Its inversion is a lower- and mid-network phenomenon — magnitude peaks at Q50 and decays above it — so restricting to the upper quartile weakens it slightly. Notably its CE correlations, which were clearly negative at the full network, sit near zero at Q75: the inversion survives only in the difference. Architecture: 128 routed experts, top-8, plus one always-active shared expert, against the dense Gemma 4 E2B (2.3B effective parameters, plus 2.8B of per-layer embeddings). That is the same dense-baseline design as every other family, so the earlier ‘only dense small model’ explanation does not apply. Gemma has the smallest compute gap in the study, 3.8B active against 2.3B (1.7×). The other low-gap family, Liquid, is also non-positive, which suggests anomalous routing marks extra gain only when the large model has substantial extra capacity. The gap does not explain why Gemma goes negative rather than to zero. Confounded by: the shared expert, which may absorb the predictable part of each token; E2B's per-layer embeddings, which give the small model token-specific capacity the compute ratio does not count; and the largest estimator spread in the study. All of these are hypotheses (tier C).

What is specific to Liquid

Liquid is quiet at Q75 as it was at the full network, and it crosses zero between them — which is a statement about how little signal there is rather than about a reversal. It remains the only family whose estimator spread stays inside the floor. Architecture: 32 experts per MoE block, top-4, with normalized sigmoid gating, on a hybrid backbone of 18 short-convolution and 6 attention blocks. The first two layers are dense, and the small model is the dense LFM2-700M. Two things limit what HC can see here. Each token yields only 32 routing p-values per layer, a quarter of Qwen's or Gemma's, which costs HC much of its power for sparse departures. And the large model applies only about 2× the small model's parameters per token, the same low gap as Gemma, so IG is small. Confounded by: the hybrid backbone, so the layer quantiles may not correspond to the same depth of processing as in the pure-transformer families.

12. Assessment

Holds up

  • Q75 is the right slice, on evidence rather than on direction. It leads every other subset on tier-A count under the bridged ESS (6 against the full network's 1) and ties for the lead at the nominal floor.
  • Qwen at Q75 is the study's clearest result. All nine benchmarks positive, 7 tier A nominally and 6 under the bridge, top cell +0.163 (+0.29 sd decile lift), and 60% retained under the Fisher control.
  • HC tracks difficulty in all four families at Q75, with the sign split that characterised the full network largely gone on the CE targets — Gemma's CE correlations move from clearly negative to near zero.
  • The stated rationale survives testing. 16 of 19 positive cells gain magnitude, and it is not regression to the mean (+0.10).
  • Sign agreement is high: 26 of 36 cells have all twelve configurations agreeing, a statistic that needs no null at all.

Not yet established

  • The selection is unadjusted. Q75 was chosen after seeing six subsets and is the arg-max in only 11% of cells. Every p-value here ignores that.
  • ERNIE's transformation is dense, not sparse. Its Q75 mean of +0.0615 goes to -0.0044 under the Fisher control, so HC adds nothing over a dense statistic there.
  • The estimator problem got worse, not better. Spread 0.0296 at Q75 against 0.0252 at the full network, with GLM -0.0206 below the rest.
  • The ESS correction is bridged, not measured. It assumes the deflation measured at full-network HC carries to Q75.
  • The boost is asymmetric, so part of what Q75 does is shift the grid positive rather than amplify signal; 10 of 36 cells change sign.
  • corr(gap, IG) = 0.96 — the restriction does nothing for the difficulty confound.

Open

  • Does the compute gap explain the family differences? The two families with a large per-token compute gap (ERNIE 10×, Qwen 5.5×) are positive and the two near 2× (Liquid, Gemma) are not. But four families cannot separate that from routing design, and the gap does not explain why Gemma inverts rather than going to zero. Every small model is dense, so the baseline does not explain it either.
  • Is the signal at Q75 sparse or dense outside Qwen? Only Qwen retains its correlation under the Fisher control, and the p_min control is unavailable at this slice entirely.
  • Why does the estimator spread widen with depth? Restricting layers should not make null estimation harder, and it does.
  • Why does lambada collapse from loudest to quietest? It is the one benchmark whose signal is strictly a full-network phenomenon.
  • Is Q75 right, or is the plateau right? Q75, Q85 and Q90 are within one tier-A cell of each other; the case for Q75 specifically is that it is the shallowest point on the plateau, not that it is distinguishable from Q85.
  • Does Gemma's inversion belong to the lower layers? Its magnitude peaks at Q50 and decays; nothing here tests why.
  • Would routing on HC pay? Best decile lift is 0.29 sd, the largest the series has produced, but no cost model exists to weigh it against.

13. Next experiments

Ranked by how much a result would change the conclusions above. Each comes from a check in section 11 that did not pass.

Pre-register Q75 and re-run on a held-out sample

P0 · ~1 day of compute, no new code
Question
Is the Q75 advantage a property of HC or of this corpus selection? Every p-value in this report ignores that Q75 was chosen after seeing all six subsets.
Design
Fix subset = Q75, estimator = GMM, variant = standard in advance. Re-run the full family × benchmark grid on a disjoint sample of each corpus, with the permutation and passage-bootstrap machinery from the 26_09_03 pipeline attached so ESS is measured rather than bridged.
Statistic
Tier counts and mean |r| on the held-out sample against 13 tier A and mean |r| = 0.0735 here.
Decision rule
If the held-out tier-A count is within ±3 of 13, Q75 is confirmed and the series should adopt it as the default slice. If it falls below 5 — the full-network count — the advantage was selection and this report has to be withdrawn.

Measure ESS at Q75 rather than bridging it

P0 · ~1 day, existing parquet
Question
Does restricting HC to upper layers change the autocorrelation of the HC series? The 2.29× deflation used here was measured on full-network HC.
Design
Compute the within-passage autocorrelation function of the Q75 HC series directly, for the same cells the 26_09_03 drop covered, and compare the resulting ESS against the full-network values.
Statistic
Q75 deflation per cell against the full-network deflation; ratio of the two.
Decision rule
If Q75 deflation is within 20% of the full-network value, the bridge in section 3 is validated and the 6-cell tier-A count stands. If Q75 HC is markedly more autocorrelated, the bridged grading is optimistic and the tier table needs recomputing.

Vary the compute ratio within one family

P1 · ~1 day, small-model forward passes only; HC is reused
Question
Does the compute gap decide whether HC tracks IG, and is Gemma's inversion a property of Gemma or of a small gap? Across families, the two pairs with a gap near 2× are the two without a positive association, but routing design varies with the gap.
Design
Hold the large model fixed and swap the dense small model, so routing design is constant and only the ratio moves. Qwen3 has a dense ladder (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B, 14B, 32B), so pairing Qwen3-30B-A3B (3.3B active) with each gives gaps of 5.5×, about 2× (the Gemma and Liquid range), below 1×, and well below. The large model's HC is unchanged, so only the small models' CE needs computing.
Statistic
r(HC, IG) at Q75 against log(active ratio), per benchmark.
Decision rule
If Qwen's r falls toward zero at the 1.7B pairing (about 2×, Gemma's gap), the compute gap is what separates the families. If it also turns negative there, Gemma's inversion is a general small-gap effect. If Qwen stays clearly positive at about 2×, the gap is not the explanation, and Gemma's shared expert or per-layer embeddings become the candidates to test.

Regenerate the p_min control and InvMinP at Q75

P1 · ~1 day, same pipeline
Question
Is the Q75 signal multi-expert? Neither the p_min control nor the single-champion statistic exists at this slice, so the question HC is built to answer cannot be asked.
Design
Extend the correlation pipeline to emit Partial_Pearson_*_diff_p_min and Pearson_Inverse_Min_P_* for Q50–Q95, not only for the full network.
Statistic
Retention under the p_min control per family, against the Fisher retention reported in section 5.
Decision rule
If Qwen retains above 0.6 under p_min at Q75 as it did at the full network (0.88), the sparse multi-expert reading holds for the chosen slice. If it drops below 0.3, Qwen's Q75 result is a single-expert effect and the HC machinery is not earning its place.

Diagnose why the estimator spread widens with depth

P1 · ~half a day, code already in the repo
Question
The spread across null estimators grows from 0.0252 at the full network to 0.0296 at Q75. Restricting layers should if anything make the routing distribution easier to fit.
Design
Compare the fitted null densities from GLM and GMM on upper-layer routing scores against full-network scores, for one cell per family. Check whether upper-layer routing is more skewed or heavier-tailed.
Statistic
KS distance between each estimator's p-value distribution and the pooled one, at Full and at Q75.
Decision rule
If upper-layer routing scores are measurably more skewed, the estimator choice should be made per slice and GLM dropped at Q75. If the divergence is unrelated to depth, every Q75 number needs an estimator sensitivity attached.

Explain the lambada reversal

P2 · a few hours
Question
lambada goes from the loudest benchmark at the full network to the quietest at Q75, the only benchmark to do so. It is also the benchmark that carried the headline Qwen result in v5.
Design
Compare token-level HC distributions at Full and Q75 on lambada against a benchmark that gains with depth (tinystories). lambada is last-word prediction with long context, so check whether its signal concentrates on the final token of each passage.
Statistic
r(HC, IG) computed on final tokens only versus all tokens, at both slices.
Decision rule
If lambada's full-network signal is carried by final tokens, the benchmark is measuring something structurally different from the others and should be reported separately throughout the series rather than pooled into dataset averages.

Token-level control for baseline difficulty

corr(gap, IG) = 0.96 at Q75, unchanged from the full network. Open across five reports now.
Design
Within deciles of CEbig, compute r(HC, IG) per stratum at Q75; separately the token-level partial r(HC, IG | CEbig). Run on Qwen's tier-A cells.
Statistic
Stratified r(HC, IG) and its spread across deciles; partial against raw.
Decision rule
If the partial retains 60% or more and the stratified estimates are stable, the 'where scale helps' phrasing becomes defensible. Below 30%, drop the IG framing for the difficulty gap.
